speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Today, vets in Singapore are licensed under the Animals and Birds Act (ABA).

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This framework has served us well in safeguarding animal health and welfare, and in protecting human health from animal diseases.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: However, our vet sector has evolved and matured significantly.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Our pet population and demand for vet services have grown.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The range and sophistication of vet services and treatment have also expanded.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In particular, there has been a rise in the number of vet specialists and breadth of vet specialisations available here in Singapore, offering specialised surgical and medical services.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Coupled with a robust professional regulatory framework, this aims to raise professional standards and uphold public confidence in our vet sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In drafting this Bill, we conducted extensive consultation with the vet sector, sought views from the public and studied models governing other human healthcare professions in Singapore and those of reputable vet statutory bodies in other jurisdictions, including Australia, Hong Kong and the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Part 1 lays out the fundamentals of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 2 defines the practice of veterinary medicine, which comprises the range of professional activities regulated by the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 3 defines who is regarded as a duly qualified vet.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Part 2 of the Bill establishes the Vet Council and sets out its functions in Clause 5.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This includes registering vets, setting standards for professional conduct and requirements for upskilling and appointing necessary bodies for disciplinary proceedings against the misconduct and negligence of vets.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 4 provides for the Council's composition, which will comprise a mix of public and private sector members.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This may include ex officio members, comprising the Director-General for Animal Health and Welfare who is a public officer, and the elected president of the Singapore Veterinary Association or their nominees and the appointed Registrar of the Council.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Registrar will be a public officer or an officer or employee of a public authority.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Council will also comprise at least four other vets and at least two other non-vets.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Members will serve a maximum term of three years and may be re-appointed.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Minister for National Development will have powers to appoint and remove members, while taking into account the Council's prevailing operating needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 13 empowers the Council to appoint committees, which will advise the Council on nascent issues, such as reviewing the Code of Ethics for Veterinarians to provide up-to-date standards on professional conduct.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Besides providing fair and adequate representation of the vet sector, which was a key feedback we received during our engagements, we also designed this framework to safeguard public interests.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It will ensure that professional regulation is grounded in practical experience with appropriate public oversight while addressing emerging issues faced by the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Part 3 of the Bill sets out structured registration and practising certification frameworks for vets.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clauses 17 to 19 provide for the registration of vets under three classes of registration, to better differentiate a vet's foundational qualification, training and practice experience.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 24 requires the Registrar to publish on the Council's website, certain particulars of the registered vets.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This enables the public to search for and verify a vet's registration status and place of practice.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is for vets who either hold a prescribed qualification or hold a qualification in veterinary medicine that is not lower in standing than the prescribed qualification and possess the necessary knowledge, skill and experience.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The prescribed qualifications mirror the Animal and Veterinary Service's (AVS's) current licensing criteria, which are accredited by well-established accrediting organisations.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The second class is vets with restricted registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Vets with restricted registration will be subjected to certain restrictions, such as to practise only under the supervision of vets with full registration or in specific establishments.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These vets must hold a qualification in veterinary medicine that does not qualify for full registration but has provided them with adequate training.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: They must also possess the necessary knowledge, skill and experience, and must be selected for employment in establishments recognised by the Council, such as the zoo or research institutes.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This allows the Council to address manpower gaps in niche domains of practice, without compromising animal health and welfare or public confidence in the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The third class of registration is specialist registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is for vets with full registration who additionally hold an approved postgraduate qualification or have acquired special knowledge, skill and experience in a particular branch of vet medicine.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Such vets will be allowed to use specialist titles, such as vet ophthalmologist or vet pathologist.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: A full or restricted registration has no expiry but may be cancelled by the Registrar or Council on any relevant grounds set out in clauses 26 and 38, or Part 5 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: A specialist registration is subject to renewals by the Council.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: To ensure vets continually improve and update their knowledge and skills, registered vets must also obtain a practising certificate from the Council to practise veterinary medicine.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Vets must regularly renew their practising certificates and fulfil mandatory continuing professional education requirements.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These requirements ensure ongoing competency, and are already in place today for AVS-licensed vets.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Council will provide more clarity on these requirements when ready.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: With these new frameworks, the public can be better informed of a vet's professional standing and competency.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: To minimise disruption to the sector and to ensure continuity of vet services, clause 90 will provide an arrangement for all AVS-licensed vets to transit to the new framework seamlessly.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For instance, the majority of existing vets will be placed on full registration as they currently hold a full licence.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Existing vets will then need to obtain registration and a practising certificate within a stipulated grace period to continue practising veterinary medicine.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Bill also ensures that services provided by certain non-vets will not be disrupted.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: As we have observed a growth in the range of animal-related services offered by non-vets that may pose a risk to animal health and welfare, Part 4 of the Bill will introduce various offences and penalties to safeguard against unlawful practice and misrepresentation by or about unauthorised persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This strengthens deterrence against profit-driven motives and was benchmarked with penalties applicable in human healthcare professions.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Apart from prohibiting unauthorised persons from practising veterinary medicine or falsely implying that they are vets and qualified to act as a vet, it will also be an offence for other persons, such as business owners and employers, to make false claims that their employee is qualified.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The prohibition of the practice of veterinary medicine by unauthorised persons garnered strong support from stakeholders and the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It also aims to better assure the public that their animals are receiving treatment from duly qualified vets.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Part 5 of the Bill introduces a robust disciplinary framework for vets, which is designed to be proportionate and impartial.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clauses 44 and 45 establish clear thresholds for escalating disciplinary cases brought against registered vets, whereby the Registrar will first triage a case against a registered vet before recommending to the Council on the action to be taken.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Registrar can recommend dismissing the case if the complaint is frivolous, so vets are not unduly burdened by unmeritorious cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: If there is evidence of physical or mental health issues which impair the vet's fitness to practise, the Registrar can recommend the Council to cancel, suspend or impose conditions or restrictions on the vet's registration with the vet's agreement.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Registrar may also recommend to the Council to refer the case to various committees, which are the (a) Complaints Assessment Committee to review the conduct of or services provided by the vet; (b) Disciplinary Committee if the vet has been convicted of an offence involving fraud, dishonesty or implying a defect in character; and (c) Interim Orders Committee to review whether to make an interim order against the vet pending inquiry into the case.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This approach ensures proportionality to the issue at hand.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Committee Members will be drawn from either a Complaints Panel appointed by the Council or from both the Complaints Panel and the Council.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The intent is for a wider pool of experienced vets to be part of the committees to contribute their clinical perspective.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Members involved at earlier stages of a disciplinary case must not sit on a subsequent committee for the same case.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These safeguards mitigate potential conflicts of interest and ensure impartiality in reviewing disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: I will highlight next, key actions or orders that may be taken by the different committees.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For minor complaints, clause 50 allows the Complaints Assessment Committee to recommend referring a case for mediation by an appointed mediator.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is one of the key features which promotes conciliatory mediation and conciliatory resolution.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This may be applied to cases involving miscommunication between vets and their clients and allow for both parties to reach a resolution through facilitated dialogue.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Cases where such interim orders may be needed include those involving serious or immediate risks to public or animal health.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Interim orders allow for swift responses to protect or secure certain interests, while disciplinary proceedings are ongoing.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clauses 51, 52, 62 and 70 provide a mechanism for appeals against certain decisions of the Council or its committees to be heard.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Minister will hear appeals against the Council's decisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This disciplinary framework broadly aligns with that for the human healthcare professions and aims to uphold public confidence in the vet sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Lastly, Part 6 of the Bill provides powers for the Council to make regulations on qualifications for registration, continuing professional education requirements and professional standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Minister's approval must be sought when regulations are made by the Council.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will give the sector sufficient time to adapt to the Bill's requirements and to strengthen their processes.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We will share more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This Bill marks an important milestone in the maturation of our vet sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It will strengthen professional accountability, support better animal health and welfare outcomes and uphold public confidence in the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Vet Council will benefit the veterinary profession, which has provided support for the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It will lead to better treatment outcomes to better safeguard animal health and welfare.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It will also benefit the public who can be more assured of the competency and quality of veterinary services, and better veterinary-client relationships.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, I would like to raise one central concern on behalf of many pet owners, which is: how do we strengthen professionalism in the sector while ensuring that vet care remains affordable and accessible?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is especially so in an ageing society, where pets can be an important source of companionship, comfort and emotional support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To many people, their pet is a source of joy, comfort and, sometimes, their daily, closest companion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, as we improve standards and professionalise the sector, we must exercise care that the new rules, guidelines and expectations do not unintentionally drive up the cost of care.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Put simply, caring for a cat or dog or any pet must not be the preserve of the wealthy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But because affordability matters so much for the ordinary pet owners, it is important we state this concern early and watch implementation carefully.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that in mind, I would like to make a few suggestions and seek several clarifications.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: First, while the Veterinary Council is a useful and necessary institution, its role under the Bill is primarily to regulate professional standards, registration, conduct and discipline.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In other words, as standards are raised, affordability should not be treated as an afterthought.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Second, I suggest that the Council, or one of its committees, should have a stronger channel for the voice of the animal welfare and pet owner interests.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This could be done either through including one or two individuals with strong standing in the animal welfare community, or through a dedicated advisory committee on affordable and accessible animal care.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This would help ensure that the system does not only hear from providers but also remain attentive to the lived realities of pet owners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am not suggesting anywhere as elaborate as the healthcare sector's fee benchmark or procedure-by-procedure guidelines.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But some basic monitoring of care and costs of care would be helpful.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Without data, we will not know whether the improvements in standards are being achieved in a way that remains sustainable for ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And if care rises in the years ahead, we should at least be able to distinguish between whether it is driven by inflation, manpower costs, or more advanced treatment norms, or regulatory and professional requirements.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Fourth, I would like to seek clarification on the disciplinary and appeals framework.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I agree that veterinarians must be held accountable for misconduct and negligence, and I support having meaningful powers to act against serious wrongdoing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we should also ensure that the process do not inadvertently encourage frivolous complaints because that can have real consequences.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If professionals feel constantly exposed to weak but career-threatening complaints, they may respond by practising defensive medicine, over-ordering procedures or face higher professional indemnity costs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And in the end, these costs may be passed to pet owners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, I appreciate clarifications from MND on how the framework will guard against misuse while preserving confidence and fairness for complainants.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I note that the Bill allows frivolous or misconstrued complaints to be dismissed, and I welcome that.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But it would be helpful to understand whether AVS expects to publish workflows, aggregate data or guidance over time, so that both the public and the professionals can have confidence that the process is balanced, transparent and not easily abused.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Fifth, as the Council develops codes, standards and professional expectations, I hope there will be deliberate attention on practical and tiered care options.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In concrete terms, financially stretched pet owners should still be able to receive clear advice upfront on what constitutes a basic, safe and affordable course of treatment, as distinct from more comprehensive or more advanced options.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Likewise, when an animal is gravely ill and recovery is unlikely, owners should not be left without an affordable and dignified path, including euthanasia where appropriate for the animals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Different owners will make different choices and many will want the best and most extensive treatment possible for their animals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But a well-functional system should always and be able to make room for realistic, humane and affordable options.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sixth, I urge some caution before we expand on the regulatory regime to other veterinary professionals and allied animal-care providers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The intent is clearly well-meaning, and I understand that this may eventually be necessary.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These issues may sit outside the four corners of this Bill, but it sits very much within the concerns of pet owners.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure many pet owners can relate to how they can somehow figure out whether they are being taken to the dog run or being taken to the vet for medical appointment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, no matter how anxious or rebellious the patient may be, it is the patience, skill and professionalism of our veterinary core that often place both the patient and its owner at ease.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, demand for veterinary services is booming, owing to the rise in pet ownership and how pets are now often regarded as a member of the family, and not just a pet per se.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Establishing the Veterinary Council as industry's professional body is therefore instrumental towards upholding the high standards expected of the profession, and a move I strongly support.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Nonetheless, this Bill arrives against a backdrop of stretched veterinary manpower, mounting public concerns about care costs and an overall pet care ecosystem that still has significant gaps.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to touch on these topics in turn in my speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition to regulating the veterinary industry, I hope that the Council would strengthen the pipeline of registered veterinarians to ease Singapore's shortage of veterinary professionals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Currently, there is no university course in veterinary science available locally.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While Ngee Ann and Temasek Polytechnics offer vet-related diplomas, they do not provide students with the pre-requisite qualifications to become a full-fledged licensed veterinarian.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To apply for a licence to treat birds and animals under the present system, one must study overseas at a veterinary school recognised either by the American Veterinary Medical Association, the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons or the Australasian Veterinary Board's Council.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If they hold a veterinary degree from a non-recognised university, they could also sit for and pass either the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons Statutory Examination, the North American Veterinary Licensing Examination or the Australasian Veterinary Examination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a costly pathway, only open to those who have the means to do so or are awarded a scholarship, discriminating against many potential veterinarians with the love and passion for helping animals from pursuing such a novel profession.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In February 2026, a Parliamentary Question was posed to the Minister for Education on whether the Ministry will work with autonomous universities to introduce a locally-offered veterinary degree in view of growing demand and reliance on overseas trained vets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The reply was that the Ministry of Education (MOE) will continue to work with the autonomous universities and sector agencies, such as MND and NParks to monitor and assess how best to meet Singapore's long-term veterinary manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I find the answer to be quite inadequate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand the arguments that Singapore's small land area means limited farm animal populations, and that there may not be sufficient scale to justify the opening up of a new programme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the question is not whether the current supply is sufficient, which increasingly appears to be insufficient, but whether the pipeline is resilient.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A profession whose entire intake depends on Singaporeans willing to bear the cost and disruption of overseas education with no guarantee of returning, is a profession with a structurally fragile supply chain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we can always start with a partnership model.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For starters, I am reminded of the double degree programme offered by the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) in biomedical sciences and Chinese medicine with Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, which began in 2005.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, NTU is launching its own four-year Bachelor of Chinese Medicine degree, which enrolled its first class of 25 students in August 2024, with plans to go up to 40 eventually.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe this is a model which we can replicate for our own veterinary degree.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Will the Government be keen to introduce a locally offered veterinary degree, in addition to strengthening the supplies of veterinarians, which is crucial in addressing the manpower gap?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope that the Council can look into plugging the brain drain faced by the industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is up nearly six-fold, from just 122 in 2006.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Demand for vet services have been rising alongside the rising incidents of pet ownership, yet every single vet in Singapore has been trained entirely abroad.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A study conducted by James Cook University and the Singapore Veterinary Association highlights that veterinary professionals are four to nine times more likely to experience depression, anxiety and stress compared to their human healthcare counterparts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Improving our local talent pipeline would therefore help plug the brain drain within the industry by spreading out the workload more sustainably, thus reducing the likelihood of burn-out.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Another issue faced by the industry is the lack of career progression, especially amongst veterinary paraprofessionals, such as nurses and technicians.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When combined with burn-out and wages in commensurate with their less-than-ideal working conditions, it has resulted in a high attrition rate and manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With plans to regulate veterinary nurses and technicians in works, I hope that the Council can develop structured opportunities for career progression and specialisation, thus boosting their wages and job prospects.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, while clause 4(3) of the Bill specifies that the Council should minimally comprise of four fully-registered veterinarians and two laypeople, there is no explicit requirement for our veterinary paraprofessionals to be represented.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given their invaluable contributions to the industry, paraprofessionals should also have a seat at the table, thus providing an avenue for the concerns to be heard.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Big conglomerates and private equity firms have recently been heavily investing and acquiring pet care chains and veterinary practices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, although dogs are allergic to chocolate, the Mars Corporation is ironically one of the biggest players in the veterinary scene.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While such clinics benefit from a flush of capital, veterinarians might have to keep a closer eye on their bottom lines and the demands of upper management, instead of their patients.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some years ago, our family adopted a dog from the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It was uncommon to find what appeared to be a purebred dog put up for adoption, but Yellow had physical deformities that required consistent and ongoing medical attention.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Towards the end of his life, the cost of managing his condition was not far from what one might expect to pay for a human specialist.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: He was family and we wanted to do everything we could to ease his suffering.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I am acutely aware that not every family is in the same position.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For some, the cost of treatment is simply prohibitive and the cruellest irony of all is that euthanasia, the most unbearable option, may also be the cheapest one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: During the consultation process of the Bill, some respondents have also raised the issue of high veterinary fees and a lack of transparency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Although regulating clinic fees is beyond the remit of the Council, I believe that there is space for the Council to act in the interest of consumer protection and to prevent runaway healthcare cost in the veterinary scene.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It will be instructive of us to study the approach taken by other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do hope the Ministry and the Council can consider regularly publishing hospital bills and fee benchmarks, similar to how the Ministry of Health has done so, or even fee guidelines for starters.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond veterinary professionals, there are others within the wider animal care ecosystem that play a key role in ensuring the health and well-being of animals, such as pet groomers and trainers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This Bill creates full professional registration, practising certificates, continuing education requirements and a multi-tiered disciplinary framework for veterinarians, like pet groomers who handle animals daily and the number of whom have been linked to dozens of investigated welfare incidents, and who, in some cases, have been responsible for animal deaths, remain largely unregulated.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There have also been cases of mishandling involving dog trainers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For instance, two employees of a dog-training firm were suspended in 2024 for physically harming two dogs under their care in preparation for a photo opportunity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Currently, pet groomers and trainers are simply required to adhere to the Code of Animal Welfare, a set of minimum standards and best practices regarding certain aspects of animal care, such as housing, feeding and transport.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back in September 2024, I asked a Parliamentary Question about whether there are plans to implement licensing requirements for pet groomers in the manner similar to pet breeders and boarders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand the Government is currently reviewing the Code of Animal Welfare with a focus on groomers as well as introducing a new chapter for dog trainers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the aforementioned instances of negligence by pet groomers and trainers highlight the need for a tighter enforcement regime for this group of professionals in addition to revising the penalties for animal cruelty and failure to fulfil duty of care to ensure that practitioners actually adhere to professional standards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I support the passage of this Bill but there is more we can do to develop a fully functional animal health and welfare ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This is a milestone for our veterinary community, a profession that has grown from just over 100 practitioners two decades ago to about 700 today.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The industry is still ripe for greater growth.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Pet ownership continues to rise and Singaporeans are more sensitive to the care of their furry companions.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Many neighbouring countries already have robust regulations for the veterinary industry, and it is opportune for Singapore to join the conversation.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As we move towards a more sophisticated regulatory landscape, we must ensure this Bill has the "claws and teeth" to protect not only the animals and their guardians, but also the dedicated professionals who serve and save them.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I wish to raise three areas of clarifications for consideration.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: First, the introduction of a specialist register is a welcome move, strengthening the trust and quality of advanced veterinary services.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We would not expect a general practitioner (GP) to perform complex orthopaedic, eye or soft tissue surgery on a human without a residency period and proper specialisation.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But these are common surgeries that general licensed vets do in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, clause 16 defines a specialist tier broadly and gives the Council greater statutory discretion to determine someone's place in this tier.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: There were concerns raised that the broadness of this tier cannot effectively motivate veterinary pursuits at the highest level.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In contrast, the Australian and New Zealand College of Veterinary Scientists stipulates a highly stratified professional qualification framework that informs their registration, including four tiers distinguishing general practitioners, members, fellows and finally, registered specialists.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The highest tier of registered specialist requires both a post-doctoral degree and years of clinical experience.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This is similar to the residency system in human healthcare medicine.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, there is a wide variety of postdoctoral degrees offered to prospective students, allowing them to upskill at the correct level of expertise and knowledge.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, the UK distinguishes between general practitioners, advanced practitioners and board-certified specialists.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Advanced practitioners have postdoctoral degrees and practical experience but still might not meet the threshold to be considered board-certified specialists who receive residency training similar to human medicine, contribute to published research and are active in the specialty.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This may risk the specialist tier being too blunt and not useful to consumers as a mark of trust and quality.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Many vets in Singapore studied in Australia and the UK.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They are already familiar with more detailed tiered systems.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: So, it is not surprising that we have received feedback that the proposed tiers could be more robust, especially in the specialist class.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: First, will the Ministry substantiate the specific requirements for the specialist tier in the subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, if we are to stick with these three tiers, how does this safeguard the public interest as effectively as more granular international models?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Third, to complement the Bill and encourage more stringent and continuous education requirements, will the Ministry consider providing support and grants to vet professionals for continuing education?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, another clarification desired on the ground is how will we protect our vets against death by process in possibly dealing with a "double penalty" of having to simultaneously defend a claim in the civil courts and a Vet Council inquiry, for the same set of facts.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that both processes serve a different purpose.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The civil courts serve to compensate for damages, and the Vet Council serves to discipline malpractice.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, vets who are likely to operate in smaller clinics would not have the resources to address two parallel processes.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: A single case could be a death sentence for the business, even if they are eventually cleared.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This is a staggering timeframe to disrupt a person's livelihood.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Accountability is important, but it must be balanced with trust in our professionals.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, we risk increasing consumer costs from defensive medicine or deterring passionate people from taking up this specialised career.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: To avoid disproportionate "punishment by process", can the Minister of State elaborate first, how does the Government balance the potential proceedings vets may face?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be guidelines to limit the amount of investigation time?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: If there are concurrent proceedings, can civil cases be put on hold until findings from the Vet Council have been released?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, vets often face "de minimis" claims – small, repetitive legal threats – that constitute a form of harassment.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has done a great job since COVID-19 to prevent and protect our healthcare workers from harassment and abuse.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We can do the same for our vets.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In the UK, this protection is extended to vets under the Respect Your Vet Team initiative.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, which is the UK's equivalent of a Veterinary Council, provides additional support to vets that makes them more than just a regulatory and disciplinary body.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons provides a hotline for vets to discuss grey area issues, support vets through difficult disputes and, in recent years, have launched numerous initiatives to champion the mental well-being for vets.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: One such initiative is the ProfCon Investigation Support that provides Confidential Peer Support for those under investigation and their flagship Mind Matters Initiative that provides workshops to promote mental well-being and mental health in the industry.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This is a small industry with high attrition rates.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Vets tend to have lower comparative pay despite years of specialised study, while managing compassion fatigue and abuse.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This is slated to worsen if individuals spend more time and money to upskill as specialists, but continue to receive similar pay and working conditions.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This shortage, in turn, transfers to the consumers, as a fall in the supply of vet services results in higher costs and fewer choices.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, this Bill represents an important milestone for our veterinary industry.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As more Singaporeans keep pets and pay greater attention to pet care, the veterinary industry is expected to continue flourishing.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Establishing a new registration system for veterinary specialists will help enhance public trust and quality in advanced veterinary services.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We would not expect a GP to perform complex specialist surgery on humans.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, in the veterinary system, the blurred boundaries between specialist and non-specialist treatment make more comprehensive regulatory mechanisms necessary.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Australian and New Zealand College of Veterinary Scientists has established a four-tiered professional qualification framework.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Many of our vets have trained in Australia and the UK and are familiar with such tiered systems.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we have received feedback suggesting that the proposed tiered system, particularly in the specialist category, still has room for improvement.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The veterinary industry has a small community but high attrition rates.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Practitioners typically require years of specialised study yet face relatively low remuneration, whilst also dealing with emotional fatigue and harassment.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: If practitioners need to invest more time and money to advance as specialist veterinarians, but remuneration and working conditions remain unchanged, this situation may further deteriorate.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The cost of manpower shortage will ultimately be passed on to consumers, as fewer veterinarians mean not only higher costs but also reduced choices.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I would also like to ask the Minister whether consideration will be given to providing veterinarians with "Industry Abuse Protections" similar to those established by the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons in the UK, to strengthen occupational safeguards for veterinary practitioners?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, I know some residents who work as veterinarians.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They not only care for pets but also help pet owners with compassion.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They tell me that when they encounter situations where owners cannot afford medical bills and are forced to surrender their pets, they continue treating these animals and find new homes for them.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Veterinary Council has the potential to elevate this industry to the next level, but without clear definition of the specialist system or support for practitioners, it would be futile.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I look forward to seeing a Council that can raise industry standards without dampening practitioners' enthusiasm. : Mr Speaker, vets do more than care for our animal companions.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They are the first line of defence for zoonotic diseases and public health.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, I have residents who are also vets and they go the extra mile.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They share with me they help pet owners who cannot afford veterinary healthcare bills and end up surrendering their pets – the vets continue to treat the animals and even rehome them to another family.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Vet Council has the potential to help grow this booming industry.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But a lack of specialist clarity or support for our vets can threaten the initiative's potential.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We want a Council that elevates standards without crushing the spirits of those who practice.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: These clarifications aside, I stand in support of the Bill.

text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.59 pm until 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This Bill provides the legal architecture to meet those expectations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While I support this Bill, my concern lies with what happens when it is enacted.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Specifically, I wish to address three areas: public awareness of the new framework, the resourcing of enforcement and the position of experienced but unlicensed animal caregivers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For the first time, pet owners will have a single authoritative register to verify that the person treating their animal is properly qualified.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: But a register is only useful if people know it exists and know how to use it.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Bill creates new legal categories that will be unfamiliar to most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A duly qualified veterinarian is defined in clause 3 as a registered veterinarian with a valid practising certificate, excluding those whose registration or certificate is suspended.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: There are three tiers of registration: full, restricted and specialist.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Each carries different conditions and scope of practice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Pet owners will need to understand what these distinctions mean in practical terms, for example, that a veterinarian with restricted registration may only practise at specific establishments or under supervision.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Under clause 29, it is illegal for an unqualified individual to practise veterinary medicine.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Under clause 30 to 33, it is an offence to falsely represent oneself or another as a qualified veterinarian.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: But these protections are only effective if pet owners know that unqualified practice is now a criminal offence and know how to report suspected violations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I would ask the Minister of State two questions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, beyond the standard communications, will the Government work with veterinary clinics, pet businesses and community organisations to bring awareness directly to the point of service?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For instance, through mandatory display of registration status at clinics, or through pet licensing touchpoints, where owners already interact with AVS.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, will the Government ensure that complaint channels are not only available, but prominently publicised so that the offence provisions under clauses 29 to 33 have real deterrent effect?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The consumer protection promise of this Bill depends not just on public education, but on the right kind of public education, one that reaches pet owners at the point of service and empowers them to use the tools this Bill provides.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Clause 79 empowers the appointment of investigators, and clause 73 sets out their powers to conduct investigations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Clause 83 allows the composition of offences, that is, settling matters out of court with a fine.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Clause 85 confers jurisdiction on magistrates' courts and district courts.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These are strong provisions, but provisions on paper do not enforce themselves.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Bill does not specify who will carry out enforcement on the ground.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: AVS under NParks will presumably continue in its existing regulatory role over veterinary clinics and animal related businesses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Investigating complaints of unqualified practice, supporting the Veterinary Council's disciplinary machinery, monitoring compliance with registration conditions and continue education requirements, and building institutional expertise in a regulatory function that has not previously existed at this scale.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I will ask the Minister of State four questions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, will there be a dedicated enforcement unit, or will these functions be absorbed into AVS' existing operations?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, how many investigators does the Government anticipate appointing in the initial years?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: And fourth, will enforcement capacity be progressively scaled up as the framework matures and eventually extend to cover veterinary nurses?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has a dedicated community of animal caregivers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They include wildlife rehabilitators who nurse injured birds and monitor otters.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They include community animal feeders who look after stray and community cats, sometimes treating minor wounds or administrating basic medication.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They include shelter workers and volunteers at animal welfare organisations, who provide day-to-day care and first response for animals in distress.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Many of these individuals have developed significant practical knowledge over years, even decades of hands-on experience.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They perform an invaluable service for animal welfare in Singapore – often without compensation and at their own expense.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Bill's definition of the practice of veterinary medicine in clause 2 is broad.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It covers diagnosis of disease or injury, medical treatment, the administration of anaesthetics, drug prescription and the issuance of professional certificates.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Under clause 29(1), it is an offence for anyone who is not a duly qualified veterinarian to practise veterinary services.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I note that the Bill does provide an important exception.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This is appropriate and I do not have any qualms with it.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, the practical boundaries of this exception remain unclear.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: What constitutes supervision in the context of community animal care, where there is typically no veterinarian on site?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: What are the prescribed conditions that will govern this exception?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Can a community caregiver clean and dress wound on a community cat without breaching the law?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Can a wildlife rehabilitator administer oral rehydration to an injured bird?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They describe activities that take place every day in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The answers will depend on the regulations that are eventually prescribed under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I ask the Minister of State four questions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, does the Government intend to exercise the exemption power under clause 86 to provide the specific carve-outs for community animal welfare activities?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: And fourth, will the Government consider developing clear, practical guidelines, distinct from the regulations themselves that explain in plain language what community caregivers can and cannot do under the new framework?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The community animal care sector in Singapore operates largely on goodwill, compassion and volunteer effort.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We should regulate to protect animals, not inadvertently criminalise the very people who have been protecting them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This Bill promises to deliver on that assurance.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: But assurance on paper must translate to confidence in practice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Pet owners must be empowered to use the register and recognise unqualified practice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Enforcement must be resourced to match the ambition of this framework and the community caregivers who have been looking after Singapore's animals long before this Bill, the volunteers who feed the community cats, nurse injured wildlife and staff our shelters must not find themselves on the wrong side of a law meant to protect the very animals they serve.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding my queries and clarifications, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This shows that the sector has grown in size, scope and complexity since then.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As pet ownership rises, the range of treatments also expands.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our laws must keep pace and this is exactly what this Bill is trying to do, by ensuring that there is qualified care given.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill matters because public concerns about animal welfare and accountability have sharpened over the years, including after high-profile incidents in the wider animal care ecosystem.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But beyond individual incidents, I observe a deeper shift that is taking place in this country.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As Singapore progresses beyond our first 60 years, our sense of compassion is also broadening.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: More people do not just only care about themselves and also just human outcomes, but they also care about the welfare of animals around them.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And I see this in every single day settings.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In Clementi for instance, some residents are deeply committed to caring for community cats' well-being.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In October 2025, I organised a convening between Clementi residents, NParks, AVS and Town Councils where views were actively and passionately aired about how animal welfare can be better safeguarded.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They speak from daily caregiving experience, they want to see these animals live well, cared for and a system that responds more compassionately and effectively.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What stood out to me was that the residents were not asking for more rules.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They were asking for clearer processes, greater empathy and a stronger confidence that the relevant systems would work well when for the animal welfare's concern.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is against this backdrop, I support the Bill because it entails guardrails for animal welfare by ensuring baseline through having needing prescribed qualifications for veterinarians.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I have three broad concerns, and I hope the Government can address.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, it is about the accessibility and talent pipeline for the veterinarian profession.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When I speak to young people about their aspirations, their responses are highly diverse.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some want to be lawyers, some want to be doctors, some want to be pilots.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But there are also some that tell me that I want to be a vet when I grow older, and this is also reflected in my recent Clementi Community Run, where a youth shared with me when she was much younger, she aspired to be an animal doctor then.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But this particular aspiration usually comes from something simple.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When I ask why, this aspiration is shaped by their lived experience.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A visit to the zoo, caring for a pet at home or even just wandering around our neighbourhood shops, looking at the pet shops.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, it is my belief that in Singapore we must be able to tell every single child that their aspirations can be realised and is not a function of their family income.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While I appreciate this Bill providing greater clarity on the qualification and registration framework for those who want to practise as veterinarians in Singapore, I would like to invite you now to join me on a journey to realise what does it take to realise this aspiration.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To be fair, the landscape has improved, because before 2018, the only way that you can pursue the relevant qualification to become a veterinarian, was to do this overseas.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, the National University of Singapore's (NUS') Life Science's concurrent programme with the University of Melbourne, Doctor of Veterinarian Medicine, or known as DVM, is a pathway to be able to get such qualification.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, it is relatively costly in terms of time, commitment and also finances.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, you need to first spend five regular semesters in NUS, then following a year in Melbourne to read the first year of DVM, continued with three more years as a full-time international student in Melbourne to complete this DVM.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There are also other hidden costs as well, such as accommodation, transportation and daily necessities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, while this is a good thing that we have at least a local-linked pathway, the financial barriers are real.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I say this not as a criticism of this Bill, because after all, this is not a higher education Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But once Parliament puts a stronger statutory framework for this particular profession, then I think it is reasonable that we ask whether we can enhance our talent development strategy in this particular sector.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I therefore ask MND, NParks and also MOE, and as well as our institutes of higher learning (IHLs), whether we can study how to be more deliberate to reduce the financial barriers before enrolling into such programmes.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This could take the form of these few things: a bonded scholarship, bursary, enhanced study grants, structured sponsorship for Singaporeans prepared to serve in the sector after graduation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If deeper institution partnership is explored over time, perhaps the Government and our IHLs can also study what are the ways to moderate cost burden for students on such concurrent programme pathways, so the overseas component does not become a decisive barrier.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, can they still pay local school fees while studying abroad, because this is quite similar to students when they go overseas for exchange.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But my question is, are they enough, relative to the cost and the length of the pathways and whether there could be more upstream support needed so that talent is not simply lost because this route is too expensive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: NParks itself has said that pet ownership is on the rise and Singapore's veterinary sector is expanding to meet this growing demand for high quality animal care.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, Singaporeans' households are keeping pets.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, I also do know of a number of Clementi residents that recently just did a career switch to go into the animal care industry.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, when we talk about building pipeline to this profession, we are not planning for a shrinking sector, because the demand looks to me like it is likely going to continue rising.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop, I also wonder whether we should consider a full local DVM programme hosted by one of our autonomous universities, as well as maybe degree partnership, where we have more locally delivered components for our current local foreign veterinary programme offerings, stronger clinical placement arrangement.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: More broadly, I want to be able to look at every single child in Singapore and say that your aspiration matters.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We have the pathways and structures to enable you to realise your aspiration and your aspiration is not a function of your family's income.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I recognise that the points that I have raised cut across the purview of several Ministries, MOE, the Ministry of Manpower, and it does not strictly fall under the purview of MND.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But in the spirit of a whole-of-Government collaboration and since this Bill established a legal framework that defines who can practise as a vet, then the broader question is, how do we develop pipeline into this profession should also be considered.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I kid you not – I hesitated for a while and I asked myself whether should I even raise this, because what I have just raised goes beyond the strict four corners of the Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But I chose to do so because I believe Singapore must be a place where passion is made possible and not quietly limited by cost constraints.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I hope the Ministry can also focus on developing wider talent pipeline for veterinary and animal care ecosystem broadly.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is because a strong animal care sector does not only run on veterinarians.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It also requires veterinary technicians, nurses, animal care workers and other support roles.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As it stands today, I am really not sure whether there are fuller ITE pathways relevant to veterinary or animal care work.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It would be helpful for the Ministry to be able to clarify this.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This matters because a good system allows people with different strengths, academic profiles and financial starting points to contribute meaningfully.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Not everyone will become a vet, but many can still play a part in this high-quality animal care ecosystem if we build proper pathways there.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My third point concerns public assurance, governance and how this framework will work in practice.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I spoke at length about pathways; now let me move to clause 18, which introduces a category known as restricted registration for individuals who may not hold qualification from prescribed universities, but they demonstrate necessary training, knowledge, skills and experience.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For pet owners and animal lovers, this clarity of this area is important because the Council is expected to also provide more details at a later point, clear public communication on what this restricted registration allows or does not allow to do matters, because it gives pet owners that level of security to know who is giving their pet care and what can they do.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I also support the composition of the Veterinary Council, which include experienced veterinarians and laypersons.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I would like to have a little bit more elaboration on what exactly are the expertise are we looking at for the layperson?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What are they expected to bring to the table?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What are the broad considerations that will guide their selection?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I would also appreciate some clarification on the requirement to have at least a fully registered vet on the Council, because it says that it must have at least 10 years of experience as a vet.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Does this mean continuous practice or cumulative practice over time?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And what reference point does experience starts counting from?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because some vets or some animal doctors might take a career break at some point and return.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The moment that they return and when they have first started, do we look at these years as part of the 10 years of experience as a vet?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On disciplinary matters, I welcome the Bill because it provides a more developed framework for complaints assessment, disciplinary committees, interim orders, investigation, appeals and penalties.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the end of the day, we want to be able to ensure that the cost of committing a crime is high enough that it will deter others from doing it.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: More broadly, I would also like to understand how the appeals framework will operate in practice.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, if a certain appeal is routed to the Minister, or where decisions are made across different stages that involves the same bodies, there may be questions about how independent and clearly separated the processes are perceived to be.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, it would be helpful if the Ministry could clarify how the framework has been designed to ensure that confidence can be maintained on both fronts.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It gives pet owners greater assurance, gives the profession clearer legal footing and gives the public stronger grounds on what standards to expect.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But the job does not end with regulation alone.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should also make pathways into this profession more accessible, make standards clearer for the public and build a system done well in preventing potential harm to our pets and our animals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Growing up with asthma, however, the doctors advised against it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, my family, especially my mother, loved animals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And when I went abroad to study, Mom seized the opportunity to adopt a miniature schnauzer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, in 2018, Carmel suffered a heart attack.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the time, we did not have a car, but lived about a half kilometre away from an animal hospital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I vividly recall carrying her trembling body and the two of us running in our flip-flops to the facility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And despite the best efforts of the vet there, we lost Carmel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My mother went into mourning for a month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For those of us that have loved and lost pets, you would understand how that feels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Mom would have spared no expense to save her beloved Carmel, even if she had been informed in advance that the chances were slim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In that instance, we had little reason to believe that the veterinary team was not trying their best to save our pet, and I am sure this is the case for almost all cases handled by animal professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In cases like these, the grieving family may seek an outlet for blame, whether justified or not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Sometimes, the vet may indeed have been negligent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other times, they, as humans, may have made inadvertent errors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Council appears similar to other professional bodies of this nature, such as the Medical Council, Law Society or Board of Architects, and will go some way toward adjudicating cases that fall into the grey areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I believe that most would agree that adjudication over sophisticated technical judgements is best undertaken by a jury of like-minded, comparably-skilled peers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the AVA can, and currently does, credibly perform this role, it will always be a continuous challenge to resource this capacity, rather than to decentralise the regulatory process to other expert voices, such as the Council.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are, of course, residual concerns, typical of all such self-regulatory settings, that such a body may choose to protect their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
