text: And even in the absence of explicit bias, the similarity of background and training may predispose such veterinarians to groupthink, imparting an implicit bias that would be more forgiving of otherwise unforgivable errors and mistakes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is no perfect solution to this, other than to point out that there are actually well understood mechanisms to mitigate such a risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Common strategies include providing an alternative channel of appeal or an escalation mechanism, should the first decision be deemed unsatisfactory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe the Bill provides as a standard for this Government's legislative approach for recourse via appeal to the Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would be interested to know if there are any plans for a second-tier peer review for Veterinary Council decisions prior to such appeal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Might the Interim Orders Committee, detailed in clause 68, be such a body seeing that they are vested with the authority to revoke, vary or replace orders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another safeguard, which is currently implicit in the Bill, is to ensure that not just the supply, but also the demand side of the equation is being represented on the Council.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: According to NParks, the public consultation accompanying the Bill did raise suggestions for broader representation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 4(3B) does stipulate that two individuals should be laypersons, but it is unclear how informed these members would be about consumer affairs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, to prevent an over-representation of large holding groups or private equity-linked roll-ups, it may be wise to also ensure that one seat be taken up by a veterinary professional hailing from an independent clinic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, this is the heart of the Bill, because a regulatory framework is only as strong as the practical implementation of fair and effective investigative actions, followed by reasonable and acceptable disciplinary procedures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, in turn, undermined her confidence in accountability of the whole process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, I am not insinuating that there were or were not lapses in her specific case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I am sure that all in this House would agree that public trust and confidence in procedure is of utmost importance, regardless of whether these procedures associated with the investigation and disposal of cases are justifiable or defensible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I note that Part 6 of the Bill does confer a substantial degree of independence and authority to investigators to go about their business, which I agree with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, I wonder if the Minister of State would be willing to share how they expect investigators to proceed with the verification process for evidentiary documents submitted to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will there be some independent corroboration of the provenance of these documents?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would the investigators seek out other credible authorities and agencies, such as the Singapore Police Force, to support the investigation process, if necessary?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will leave us with one final thought, albeit slightly outside the formal scope of the present Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond veterinary practice, we must also continue to refine our laws that protect the welfare of animals in line with the spirit of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As of March this year, this is still ongoing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are many instances, especially when we go about our estate management matters, where we often need to take difficult decisions about prioritising our residents' legitimate concerns about noise and hygiene against the desire to cherish animals that live alongside us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, in any advanced society, we must hold ourselves to a standard of how we treat other living things in our midst.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This principle becomes even more stark when, as is often the case with veterinary services, we are dealing with the lives of animals that are often regarded as part of the household.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This Bill is a natural step in ensuring that our furry friends and family are treated right by those tasked with their physiological well-being.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, this Bill speaks to something I have seen very clearly in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How trust in a profession is built – and how easily it can be eroded if we are not careful.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Tengah, many of my residents are young families and many have pets.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They tell me they want more places to walk with them, to sit with them after a meal, to let them run safely.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It reflects something simple: that pets are part of everyday life.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But when something goes wrong, the conversation changes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One resident told me she hesitated when her pet needed treatment – not because she did not care, but because she was not sure what she was agreeing to.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And I think many people will recognise this.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because when something goes wrong, it is not just the bill that people worry about, it is whether they are making the right decision at all.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because at its core, this Bill is about trust.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But in practice, people do not read regulations.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They read people and they trust what they see in front of them.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are the foundations of a profession that people can have confidence in.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But if we are serious about trust, then we must also be very deliberate about how we design it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Council will shape standards, oversee conduct and influence how the profession evolves.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It must be credible to the profession and it must be trusted by the public.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That means having the right mix of expertise across different areas of practice and processes that are clearly fair and impartial.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It also means that where serious disciplinary findings are made, that they are communicated with sufficient clarity, so that both professionals and the public understand what is expected.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because if people cannot see how standards are applied, they will not feel assured that they exist.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second is clarity in qualifications and titles.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For most people, trust begins with what they see – a name, a designation, a title.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And the reality is this: most people will not know the difference between one qualification and another, but they will live with the consequences.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, what matters is not just how qualifications are assessed, but how clearly they are understood.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There should be transparency in what is recognised, how specialist titles are determined and what these mean in practice.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because a title can reassure, even when it should not.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And if we are not careful, that reassurance can be misplaced.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The third is how we approach restricted practice.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They allow entry into the profession while maintaining safeguards.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But we must be careful, because if we are not careful, what starts as a pathway can quietly become a standard.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, there must be clarity on scope, on progression and on how competence is assessed over time.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And we should think carefully about who is entrusted to train others, because who we allow to train matters – that is how standards rise or slip.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a safeguard and that principle applies just as strongly here.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But it is also where intent and implementation can diverge.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If it becomes a matter of ticking boxes rather than strengthening practice, then we risk losing its purpose.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, as this framework develops, it will be important to ensure that it remains meaningful, relevant and reflective of how practice continues to evolve.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not simply that veterinary costs are expensive.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not just that care is expensive.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is that people do not know where it will end.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Once they say yes, they feel like they have to keep saying yes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And that is a difficult position for any family.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Not because they do not love their pet but because they are unsure.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And over time, that uncertainty changes how people feel about the entire system.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because when people do not understand the costs, they begin to question the care.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And that is something that we should not allow to take root.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Care today is no longer delivered by one person alone.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is delivered by teams – veterinarians, nurses, rehabilitation professionals and many others.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because good professionals matter, but the system around them matters just as much.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But the real measure of its success will not be in what we pass today.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will be in what people experience tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because, in the end, how we treat animals says something about us.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But how we organise care, that says even more.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the Bill and I look forward to the Minister of State’s response on these points.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, do you have a clarification of your previous speech?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I just wish to state for the record that it was an "and" as a conjunction and not "in".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, the Bill sets up Singapore's first Veterinary Council and the aim to raise standards is welcomed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But every Council member is picked by a Minister who can remove any member for any reason.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He has the final appeal against the Council's recommendations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Why depart from that statutory elected member model here and what safeguards ensure vets have a real voice in their own oversight?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The consultation outcome did promise to include veterinary professionals on the Council but unlike the Medical Registration Act and the Dental Registration Act, the Bill does not make that representation statutory.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Regulatory costs that are marginal for a large chain can be more significant for a small practice.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Section 87(3) states, "Regulations made under this Act may make different provisions or prescribe different fees for different classes of persons or different circumstances", and all regulations require the Minister's approval under sections 87(1) and 87(2).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will the Ministry commit to using the differential fee power in section 87(3) to ensure that regulatory costs do not accelerate the consolidation the vet profession is already experiencing?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Since no regulation the Council makes can take effect without the Minister's approval, I would urge the Ministry to assess before granting that approval, whether compliance costs fall proportionately on small practices relative to their fixed cost base, and to require the Council to invoke section 87(3) where they do not.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, the Bill sets the standard but there can be multiple paths to meet it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When Member Ms Valerie Lee asked MOE in February 2026 about introducing a local veterinary science degree, the reply was that MOE would monitor and assess.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I, like my colleague, Mr Louis Chua, and Member Mr David Hoe support the idea of a local vet degree.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the goal is higher standards, why not build a local training path that can better guarantee those standards and give Singaporeans who want to become vets a route that does not need a costly overseas degree.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is a strong regional case for this.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And in advance of 25 April, I would like to wish all our vets, vet nurses and everyone who works with animals, "Happy World Veterinary Day".

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As a fellow pet owner, I believe this legislation is both timely and essential.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It rightly acknowledges the critical role the vets play, not just in safeguarding animal health but also in providing a peace of mind to families who entrust their beloved pets to their care.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: With the increasing prevalence of pet ownership and our rising expectations for animal welfare, establishing a clearer and more robust framework for this profession is a necessary and forward-thinking step.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I commend the Government for bringing this important Bill forward.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As this field continues to evolve, it is crucial that we ensure law enhances standards without inadvertently placing undue pressures on the sector.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For many Singaporeans, practical concerns loom large – the affordability of the bills, the meaningful and insurance options, the adequacy of local training for future vets and the presence of a reliable safety net for severe complications.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, while I wholeheartedly support the Bill, I urge the Government to use this opportunity to think more broadly about the sector.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, a significant concern for many pet owners is the escalating cost of the bills.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: While most owners are committed to providing responsible care, the cumulative expenses of diagnostic tests, surgeries, hospital stays and follow-up treatments can lead to unexpected and substantial bills.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For some families, this presents a genuine affordability challenge, sometimes forcing them to delay or decline necessary treatment or to struggle financially even when they wish to do the best for their fur-child.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As we elevate professional standards, it is equally important to explore ways to make the care more accessible and manageable.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I hope the Government will investigate strategies to improve affordability and price transparency, ensuring that pet owners are not left feeling shocked or helpless when critical medical interventions are required.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, insurance and whether there should be a compensation fund.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The role of insurance in mitigating the financial impact of veterinary care is undeniable.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: However, many pet owners may lack clarity on the available policies, their precise coverage or the practicalities of making their claims.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I believe the veterinary sector should explore a similar industry-wide pooled fund as a last resort, ensuring that pet owners are not left without a practical remedy when unforeseen and severe circumstances arise.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, as the profession evolves, advertising should be approached with care.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: While some degree of advertising may be acceptable, it should also be governed by stringent ethical guidelines.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: They involve professional judgement, public trust and the welfare of animals.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Advertising should therefore be free from misleading claims, exaggeration or aggressive techniques and this could pressure clinics into prioritising commercial competition over professional standards.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I propose that the Government implement an advertising framework that ensures fairness for all veterinarians, avoiding any tilt in favour of larger corporate entities with greater marketing resources.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Such a move would help prevent smaller, independent practices from being disadvantaged, thereby preserving the diversity, sustainability and competitive balance within the sector.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Furthermore, an uncontrolled increase in marketing competition would inadvertently drive up business costs, which may ultimately be passed on to pet owners.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, I urge the Government to ensure that any framework for the vets’ advertising is underpinned by robust ethics safeguards, maintaining the professionalism, fairness and long-term sustainability for the sector.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Fourth, the pipeline of future vets and whether Singapore should move towards a local vet school.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As spoken by many of my colleagues in this Parliament, if we want a strong veterinary profession in Singapore, we must not think just about regulations.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We should also think about training and about the future pipeline of vets.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today, Singapore still relies heavily on overseas education.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: While the National University of Singapore has a pathway linked to the University of Melbourne, it is not the same as having a fully local veterinary degree and training system here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I also ask whether the statistics support opening a full-time vet school in Singapore and if so, how would such a school or course be regulated, how clinical training would be supervised, and how specialist training would fit within the registration framework under this Bill.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we care about standards, access and long-term resilience, then the pipeline matters.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A stronger local pathway can help Singaporeans and Singapore build a deeper bench of veterinarians with local knowledge and long-term commitment.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I also want to raise one specific issue on the disciplinary framework under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is serious stuff, affecting livelihood, reputation and the right to practise.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Where powers of this seriousness are exercised, it would be good to have a legal professional on the Interim Orders Committee to provide safeguards against procedures and substantive irregularities and errors and to uphold rules of fairness and procedural justice during disciplinary proceedings for vets.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Every profession has a role to play in social responsibility.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In a sector that intersects with both animal welfare and the well-being of households, we should explore the potential for pro bono or community veterinary support, particularly for lower-income pet owners, urgent welfare cases and rescue organisations.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I am not suggesting an obligatory burden on every clinic.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But the sector, in collaboration with the Government, could explore more structured support mechanisms for genuine cases of need.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This would enable the Ministry to track such contributions and foster a stronger culture of service and community engagement among veterinarians.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A truly effective veterinary service system is one that not only regulates professionals adeptly but is also one that ordinary Singaporeans trust, understand and access.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It must provide robust protection for the public in serious situations, strengthen our local pipeline of future veterinarians, ensure disciplinary powers are wielded with appropriate safeguards and maintain a fair and sustainable professional landscape as the sector continues to evolve.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For all these reasons, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan, you have a clarification for a Member who has spoken before you?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I just wanted to clarify with the Member, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, with regard to the statements he made earlier on about Part 5 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This in turn undermined her confidence in the accountability of the whole process".

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is an important clarification because it also calls into question the standard of AVS and our officers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I would like for the Member to qualify this, because he also mentioned that there is at least one resident.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, would you like to reply to that invitation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This was an incident where the resident had filed multiple appeals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am sure that you can check with the Ministry with regard to the chain of events.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And that is why I supported Part 6 of the Bill which confers a degree of independence and authority to investigators to go about the process of investigation, which I am sure in her case would lend her greater confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I also wanted to share a point she had also asked me to share – about ensuring that the verification process for evidentiary documents submitted to the authorities would also involve some degree of independent corroboration about the provenance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I have mentioned those in my speech and I will reiterate that here.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan, would you like to respond to that?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I agree with you that public confidence and trust is important.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we will get back to the Member and if the Member has any further queries, please feel free to direct them to me, so we can verify.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, to be fair to you, is there anything else you wish to add in response?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: No, Speaker, other than to just point out once again that I was not taking a position that questions the professionalism of AVS, but rather representing her sentiments which, as I mentioned in my speech, when you are a grieving parent to a fur-baby, you might understandably be aggrieved and wish to look for an outlet.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This Bill is timely, because veterinary care today sits at the intersection of animal welfare, public trust and public health.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we have seen, as pet ownership rises, so too there are expectations of care.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our regulatory framework must keep pace, not just to deter poor practice, but to protect good professionals and strengthen confidence among pet owners and the wider community.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This number reflects a sector and a public that both care deeply about standards, fairness and clarity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This Bill too advances that direction in a very structured way.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I will raise three points, in the spirit of strengthening implementation, so that the Bill uplifts standards while preserving access and trust.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These efforts work best when they are matched by a professional framework that keeps the standards clear, trusted and consistent.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we raise standards, we should also keep a close eye on a very simple reality.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If standards rise while supply tightens, the lived outcome for pet owners may be longer waits, higher costs and delayed care.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This of course is not the intent of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It allows the Council to impose conditions on registration, including supervised practice, performance review, limits to setting and limits to scope for defined periods, to support safe entry and progression.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this regard, I would like to seek the Ministry's clarification on two practical areas.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, how will recognition pathways, including for overseas-trained veterinarians, be made clear and predictable, while maintaining standards.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Bill provides for prescribed qualifications, and also for Council assessment of other qualifications and competence, including examinations where appropriate.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Clear published guidance will reduce uncertainty and support consistency.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is similar to the First and Second Schedules of the Medical Registration Act, where both local and overseas qualifications are listed.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, what complementary measures will support retention and career development?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Regulation is not only about disciplining errant practice; it is also about sustaining the workforce so that good professionals can stay and grow.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I would not like to belabour the point but like to echo the points made by colleagues in the Chamber earlier that for the longer-term pipeline, I really hope that MOE and the relevant agencies can keep under review whether there may be a case for a locally administered veterinary degree.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It should also widen the pathways for capable people to meet that bar, safely and fairly.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, my second point relates to affordability and consumer trust.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The consultation feedback reflected public concerns about transparency and the pricing of veterinary services.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While I do agree that the Veterinary Council itself should not be the price setter, but affordability is shaped by more than just price controls.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is shaped by transparency, clear communication and the confidence pet owners have when making often difficult decisions under time pressure.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When treatment plans are especially complex and costs are uncertain, asymmetry between provider and consumer can lead to disputes, mistrust and delayed care.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That certainly does not help animal welfare, and it does not help the profession.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, even if fees are outside this Bill's scope, I encourage the Ministry and the Council to consider what can be done, through professional standards and guidance, to strengthen transparency in practice, clearer expectations around communication of options of treatment, informed consent and upfront cost discussion, especially in urgent or high-stakes situations.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is again similar to the medical practice where financial counselling requirements come under Healthcare Services Act.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is not about policing fees but is about strengthening trust through clarity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This Bill defines what constitutes the "practice of veterinary medicine" and draws boundaries around key acts that require professional judgement, such as diagnosis, surgical treatment, prescription and certification.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, the consultation outcome makes clear that specified groups, including students and other persons such as nurses, may perform a specified scope of activities under prescribed conditions and supervision.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It protects animals and the public by keeping core judgement where it belongs, while allowing team-based care to scale safely in a protected environment.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, provide clear and plain guidance on safe delegation and team-based workflows, including what may be done under supervision, what documentation is expected, and how accountability is preserved.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, I note the stated longer-term intention to regulate veterinary nurses, with an adequate transition period.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A phased approach is sensible, allowing engagement, capability building and continuity of services while raising standards across the wider care team.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Good regulation is not only how strongly we deter misconduct.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is how confidently good professionals can practise and how clearly citizens can navigate that system.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I also note the importance of clarity in the roles of institutions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Over the past decade, Singapore society has witnessed an obvious change, especially during and after COVID-19, and that is more and more families have begun keeping pets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Whether in HDB communities or private residential areas, we can see increasing numbers of residents walking their pets, taking them to see a vet, or participating in community activities with them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For many families, pets are no longer just animals, but important companions in their lives.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some treat pets as friends, others as family members.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I have a friend who owns a medium-sized dog shared with me his story.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: He said that when he gets a haircut, it costs around $20, but when his dog gets grooming care, it costs over $100 dollars.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The annual pet insurance alone costs several hundred dollars.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Adding up the daily expenses for treats, supplies and basic care, it amounts to a considerable sum.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Yet despite this, many people are still willing to continue keeping dogs, cats and other pets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because for them, this is no longer simply about keeping an animal – they truly regard them as family members.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As the saying goes, humans have emotions and animals do too.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When society's attitude towards animals gradually changes, our systems also need to keep pace with the times.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: From basic vaccinations and health checks to surgical procedures and specialist treatments, Singapore's veterinary services industry is continuously developing and becoming more specialised.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop, establishing a clear, comprehensive and credible veterinary regulatory framework becomes extremely important.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When pets become family members, people's expectations of veterinary services naturally increase.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A clear, fair, and professional regulatory system can not only protect animal health and welfare, but also safeguard the rights of pet owners.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The ancients often said: when systems are established, people's hearts are at ease.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When the public knows that an industry has clear standards, oversight, and accountability mechanisms, society's trust in the entire industry will also improve accordingly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With increasing pet numbers and increasingly specialised pet medical services, Singapore's future demand for veterinary talent will likely continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond regulation, should we also simultaneously consider how to attract more young people into the veterinary profession through education, training and professional development opportunities, and support local veterinarians in continuously enhancing their professional capabilities?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Can we encourage local universities to set up veterinary degrees?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Often, whilst institutions have been established, the public may not fully know how to utilise them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If the public is unclear about the differences between full registration, restricted registration and specialist registration, the Bill's protective function may be diminished in practice.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Thirdly, as pet medical technology continues to develop, the industry is gradually seeing specialist services and high-end medical care.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Will the Government consider in future how to encourage professional industry development whilst also ensuring service accessibility and reasonable transparency?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I believe this is also a concern for many pet owners.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many people are willing to invest in their pets and take responsibility, but they also hope for clearer communication, more transparent explanations and a stronger foundation of trust when facing treatment and medical advice.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Fourthly, beyond regulating veterinarians themselves, will there be continued review of other professional services related to animal care in future, to ensure the entire ecosystem clearly distinguishes the responsibility boundaries between professional medical care, basic care and other auxiliary services?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today's pet industry development encompasses not just clinics, but also care, grooming, boarding, rehabilitation and other related services.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If boundaries are unclear, the public may sometimes be confused about which services involve professional medical judgement, and which do not.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When we are willing to provide better medical care for animals and establish more professional and responsible industry regime, it reflects society's respect for life.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As more Singaporeans welcome pets into their homes, animals are increasingly regarded not merely as companions, but as members of the family.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, I hope we will continue to ask how the framework can be supported in practice.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These are important questions as we move forward.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It strengthens animal welfare by ensuring veterinarians are held to high professional standards.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It builds public trust through mandatory licensing and clearer processes for managing feedback and complaints.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nevertheless, I would like to raise some points for the Ministry's consideration.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, I would like to ask what steps the Ministry will take to attract and retain talent in our veterinarian industry.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This translates to roughly one veterinarian for every 1,186 animals, with some of the 674 not working full-time.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The profession has expanded, but it has not kept pace with demand.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also suffers from high stress, long hours and burn-out, driving many local vets to work in Australia or the UK.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The brain drain has a direct knock-on effect on costs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Vet fees rose by up to 20% in 2022.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill's additional regulatory requirements risk compounding this, adding compliance burdens that may deter talent from entering or staying in the profession.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry consider expanding the list of recognised overseas veterinary qualification and exploring Singapore-based pathways to licensing, so that aspiring vets are not compelled to study abroad and potentially settle there?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is currently only one non-profit community animal clinic in Singapore, run by the SPCA, serving pet guardians in financial hardship, supplemented by ad hoc free health screenings for lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is insufficient for our growing pet population.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would highlight two groups that we might consider subsidies for.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Vet bills have risen over 30% since 2022.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Subsidised veterinary care for adopted rescue pets from approved rescuers could incentivise adoption and relieve pressures on overstretched shelters.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Animals serving an assisted function deserve some considerations too.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Guide dogs for the visually impaired, or therapy animals that provide genuine medical and social value.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While Guide Dogs Singapore subsidises some routine care, some financial burden on dog owners remains significant.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry consider formalising support for these animals?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, I would like to ask the Ministry to clarify the scope of practices that must be performed by a licensed veterinarian, in particular, whether the regulation of pet groomers or practices in the ornamental fish industry can be considered alongside the Bill.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is no legal requirement for pet groomers to be professionally trained or certified.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have also heard about the tragedies – the death of Fendi the Corgi, who choked during a grooming session; the ACRES White Paper last year had also flagged concerns about the unregulated industry.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a growing grey area where grooming shades into veterinary practice.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, when a groomer handles a pet with an existing skin condition or infection.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fish cosmetic surgery is a particularly stark example of invasive procedures carried out without medical oversight.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, Arowana fish are routinely subject to eye lifts, chin jobs, scale shaving and swim bladder repairs by non-vets.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A Singapore aquarium magazine also once published a step-by-step guide to tail amputation on Flowerhorn cichlids using scissors without anaesthetic and dye injection into Parrot cichlids using hypodermic needles.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of these aesthetic services continue to be openly publicising in the ornamental fish industry.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry or Veterinary Council issue clear guidelines on which procedures might need a licensed vet and consider a basic certification framework for pet groomers?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A related concern is the rise of non-conventional animal therapies – from stem cell treatments to administering horse injections, medications to dogs and cats – amplified by social media.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: AVS and the Singapore Veterinary Association in this regard, have jointly published the Veterinary Therapeutic Guidelines in response and these remain voluntary.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry consider empowering the Veterinary Council to enforce minimum standards for non-conventional therapies, protecting pet owners from treatments that are unproven or potentially harmful?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fourth, the Bill will first apply to veterinarians before eventually extending to veterinary nurses.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the Veterinary Council was originally slated for establishment last year and was delayed.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry provide a concrete timeline for when veterinary nurses will be brought under the framework, so the profession can anticipate and plan accordingly?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This also aligns with pricing transparency, where the Veterinary Therapeutic Guidelines already recommend that vets provide clinics with cost estimates and disclose the evidence base for such treatments, but this is currently voluntary.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I support this Bill and look forward to the Ministry's response.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ms C, a Yio Chu Kang resident, is one of them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She has even helped to organise pet shows and events in our constituency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A few years ago, when her dog passed away, it was a very difficult time for her.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When I visited her again recently, she showed me photos, paintings she had kept and even a tattoo of her dog's name on her arm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For her and for many Singaporeans, animals are no longer just pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When a family member falls ill, we do not ask for the bare minimum.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The establishment of the Veterinary Council, with powers to register vets, set standards, accredit training and enforce discipline, is a significant step towards professionalising the sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The tiered registration system and continuing professional education requirements will raise standards across the board.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, residents will ultimately judge this Bill not by its structures, but by whether it gives them the confidence at the point of care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, vet services must remain affordable and accessible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Pets are a source of emotional support for seniors, children and families with special needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond households, community caregivers, independent rescuers and animal shelters pay out of their own pockets to care for animals which may not even be their own.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, the cost of veterinary care has become a growing concern.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For chronic conditions, such as kidney or liver failure, it is not uncommon to see caregivers crowdfunding five-figure sums to save an animal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To be fair, vets face rising costs in commercial rent, diagnostic equipment and imported medicines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But recognising these pressures does not resolve the burden on residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Affordability was one of the most prominent concerns raised during the public consultation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, veterinary fees fall outside the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From the resident's perspective, regulating quality without a concrete affordability and transparency roadmap feels incomplete.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Pet owners experience quality and price at the same counter, often during a stressful emergency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Why should they wait for a future policy response when this concern is already well-established?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If stronger regulations increase compliance and operational costs, what assurance do we have that households will not face even steeper bills?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, while we wait, can we mandate fee transparency immediately?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Council also publish fee benchmarks so that people know the sort of ranges to expect and for other vets to benchmark themselves, like in the medical sector?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, will the Ministry actively monitor whether the implementation of this Bill correlates with rising consumer costs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, will the Ministry work with the industry to help manage the underlying drivers of these costs, such as commercial rent and medicine procurement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Access does not begin at the clinic door.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, residents want a competent team to treat their pet.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When a family hands over their pet for a major procedure, they face a sobering reality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is always a risk that the animal may never wake up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because the stakes are high, they want assurance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill defines the practice of veterinary medicine broadly but allows certain acts to be performed by non-vets under supervision.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Importantly, high-risk procedures, such as the administration of anaesthesia are not excluded.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, the regulatory framework for veterinary nurses and paraprofessionals is not yet in place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Council is tasked with setting standards and requiring continuing professional education for vets, but the paraprofessionals assisting them remain in legislative limbo.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What does "under veterinary supervision" mean in practice for high-risk procedures?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is this supervision direct, on-site and immediate or merely general supervision or consultation should any issues arise from another room?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If a veterinary nurse is permitted to administer anaesthesia under supervision, what competency assurance exists right now, before their regulatory framework is in place?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry clarify when these additional provisions relating to paraprofessionals, will be introduced?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry commit to publishing the supervision guidelines before the main operational provisions of this Bill commence?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Council provide a clear, public list of high-risk acts requiring tighter, direct vet involvement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When the risks and corresponding costs are high, clarity cannot be left to interpretation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, residents need clear and accessible information to make informed choices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill introduces a structured registration system of full, restricted and specialist categories.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, the information currently made available to the public is limited to name, place of practice, qualifications and registration date.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Vice Chair of the Health Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC), I have seen how transparency builds trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In human medicine, the Singapore Medical Council provides a clear benchmark.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The public can check a doctor's registration type, specialist branch, practising certificate status and active conditions or restrictions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we treat our pets like family and vets like professionals, residents deserve a similar level of clarity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Pet owners should not need specialist knowledge just to understand who is qualified to do what, right now.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, when things go wrong, residents must have confidence that they can seek redress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill establishes a structured disciplinary process with safeguards like layperson involvement and conflict-of-interest rules.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But from a grieving resident's perspective, the process may still feel intimidating.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A disciplinary case must be supported by a statutory declaration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For an ordinary resident, this is not a mere administrative step.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the start of a formal legal process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be clear guidance and simpler templates so genuine grievances are not deterred?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Relatedly, what are the expected processing times for Complaints Assessment Committees and Disciplinary Committees, and are there clear service standards?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, given that individuals may still pursue civil claims through the Courts, what role does this disciplinary framework play in practice and what would encourage the public to use this process instead of going directly to Court?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be a firm commitment to publish disciplinary workflows and final outcomes, so complainants are not left feeling shut out?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Appeals against certain Council decisions go to the Minister, who also appoints and may remove Council members.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I do not doubt the integrity of our institutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But how does this structure ensure perceived independence in the eyes of the public?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In particular, why do appeals from the Complaints Assessment Committee need to be heard by the Minister?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there scope for these to be adjudicated by an independent tribunal instead?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Deputy Speaker, we must ensure inclusivity for vets for easy compliance, while maintaining high standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How frequently must practising certificates be renewed and what criteria will be used to assess renewal?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Council continually review the list of accredited qualifications and recognised schools to ensure standards remain current and internationally benchmarked?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Further, how will older vets transition into this new system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If processes are primarily digital, what support will be provided to ensure senior practitioners are not left behind?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, how would representation within the Veterinary Council reflect the diversity of the profession?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For her, caring for her dog was never just about fun.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Her deep love for her pets is not uncommon.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, pet owners have parted with life savings to save their pets, hired help or sacrificed travel and career opportunities to care for ill and ageing pets, as they would for their family members.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the question before us is no longer just about animals or pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about how we care for those we consider family.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if that is the case, then the questions raised in my speech are not abstract.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are about whether care is affordable, so families can say yes without fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are about whether care is competent, so families can trust those treating their pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are about whether care is transparent, so families can make informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are about whether care is accountable, so families know the system will be fair when something goes wrong.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But a framework alone does not create confidence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Confidence is built when access is real, when responsibility is clear, when information is transparent and when accountability is trusted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because trust is not created by regulation alone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is created when systems work for people, when processes are clear and when outcomes are fair.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, let us take this opportunity to do more than regulate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us ensure that no family hesitates because of cost and that no resident is left uncertain about who is responsible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us also ensure that no one feels shut out when seeking accountability and let us build a system that residents can rely on, not just in principle, but in practice.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Deputy Speaker, I rise in support of the Bill, which seeks to provide for the registration of veterinarians and the regulation of individuals practising veterinary medicine.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This Bill reflects how we, as a society, value animal welfare, professional standards and consumer trust.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As Singapore's pet scene evolves and grows, our vet care systems and regulatory framework must evolve in tandem.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In this regard, the Bill is both timely and necessary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I would like to raise several questions and suggestions, particularly from the perspectives of workforce development and consumer protection and, at the same time, to draw on relevant practices from other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Pets today, as many Members of the House have mentioned, are no longer just companions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With this shift has come a corresponding rise in expectations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Owners seek not only competent care, but also high standards of professionalism, communication and accountability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many pet owners are also prepared to invest more to ensure the well-being of their animals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As a pet owner myself, I can certainly relate to this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We all want to do our best for our pets, especially when they are unwell or vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In this context, the establishment of a Veterinary Council is an important step forward.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It will strengthen governance, uphold standards and enhance public confidence in vet services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Vet nurses, technicians and allied professionals are integral to diagnosis, treatment and recovery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They are often the first point of contact for pet owners and play a critical role in ensuring continuity of care.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: From a Labour Movement perspective, it is important that these workers are not treated as peripheral, but as professionals in their own right.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This means having clear standards of practice, structured training and certification pathways, fair wages and working conditions and meaningful career progression.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Without these, we risk a situation where demand continues to grow, but the workforce remains stretched, under-recognised and difficult to retain.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we look at developments overseas, the direction is clear.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Hong Kong, the authorities are studying a framework to regulate veterinary nursing practitioners.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Similarly, in the UK, reforms are moving towards stronger recognition and oversight of allied veterinary professionals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These developments suggest that a modern vet system does not focus only on vets, but also on the entire care team.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But the question is whether it will be done through accreditation, registration or other mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And the more important question is, when will it take place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such a framework would not only uplift the profession but also give consumers greater assurance about the competency of the entire care team.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, the pathway to becoming a vet remains largely dependent on overseas training, such as the concurrent programme between NUS and the University of Melbourne.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While this has served us well, it may not be sufficient to meet growing demand, particularly as veterinary services become more specialised.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There are also barriers in terms of cost and accessibility.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Not all aspiring Singaporeans may have the means to pursue overseas education.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: From a workforce development perspective, we should consider whether more can be done to strengthen local pathways: whether through expanded partnerships, local clinical training opportunities, or, in the longer term, a local degree option.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At the same time, we should continue to support and to develop our local pool of vet nurses and technicians, who form the backbone of our day-to-day care.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A strong, well-supported workforce across all levels is essential if we are to deliver consistent, high-quality vet services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Vet care can be a significant and sometimes, unexpected expense for households.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Pet owners often have to make decisions under emotional stress, with limited information and time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This creates a situation of information asymmetry, where consumers may not always be able to fully assess treatment options or costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, trust must be supported by systems: by transparency, accountability and fair practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Feedback from the public has highlighted concerns about the lack of upfront price clarity, wide variations in fees and difficulty in comparing services across providers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In this regard, we should look at developments in the UK.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Hong Kong, the regulatory body has introduced clearer expectations on client communication, including guidance on what should be conveyed to pet owners before treatment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This includes information on diagnosis, treatment options, risks and estimated costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such practices recognise that consumers should be properly informed before making decisions, especially where procedures may be complex or costly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would therefore like to ask whether similar guidance or professional standards on informed consent will be developed here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask whether the composition of our Vet Council will similarly incorporate, or formally consult, consumer or public-interest perspectives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will help ensure that the regulatory framework is not solely profession-led, but also grounded in the needs, expectations and protection of consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Internationally, there is increasing recognition that regulation should not only be disciplinary, but also developmental – supporting professionals to improve and maintain standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: International experience shows that a modern vet system goes beyond regulating individuals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It builds a professional, accountable and consumer-centric ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By moving in this direction, we can develop a vet sector that is not only professionally robust, but also fair, sustainable and trusted by the public.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I learnt many different things: Members' love for their pets and animals, including Carmel, Yellow; and also about fish cosmetic surgery, including eye lifts and chin jobs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Please allow me to address Members' comments via four broad themes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The first theme is on representation of the Veterinary Council.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Veterinary Council will perform an essential role to regulate our vet sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Its primary duty is to register vets, set and maintain high standards for the practice of veterinary medicine in Singapore and appoint necessary bodies for disciplinary proceedings to safeguard animal health and welfare as well as the public interest.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In that regard, I agree with Dr Choo Pei Ling that Council members should have the right mix of expertise to fairly and adequately represent the vet sector and to set the high standards that is expected of the vet sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is why this Bill provides for the Minister to appoint a balanced composition of members.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I shared earlier that the Council may include ex-officio members from the public and private sectors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Considering public feedback that we have received through the consultation process, we intend to also appoint suitably experienced vets from diverse areas of the vet sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This will allow us to strengthen the development of professional standards that enhance and advance the vet sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We intend to nominate legal professionals from the start because this helps provide wider perspectives and ensure the reflection of broader public interest in the Council's work.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There will also be Government oversight of key aspects of the Council for alignment with public interest and accountability, and I will elaborate on these later.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Over time, we will review the Veterinary Council's operating needs and adjust its composition accordingly.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This may include appointing other vet professionals, such as vet nurses, further down the road.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This could include key representatives of animal groups to share feedback with the Council as Mr Henry Kwek and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggested.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second theme of questions surround the new registration and practising certificate framework, which Mr Cai Yinzhou, Ms Lee Hui Ying and Dr Choo Pei Ling raised questions on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Bill defines the practice of veterinary medicine, which can only be performed by duly qualified vets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But in line with feedback that we received from the vet sector, the Council intends to recognise specialist vets primarily based on postgraduate degrees or qualifications, and will publish the requirements on its website when ready.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we will start with this new three-tiered registration framework and then monitor its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are also open to exploring other approaches to further recognise as well as to differentiate vets where necessary.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With regard to Ms Diana Pang's suggestion, the Bill will not require vets to declare their pro bono hours as part of the practising certificate renewal requirements.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we appreciate that vets regularly volunteer their time and efforts, such as in sterilisation and microchipping drives on a pro bono basis, and we will explore other ways to recognise their goodwill and their generosity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Lee Hong Chuang, Dr Choo Pei Ling, Ms Diana Pang, Mr David Hoe, Dr Hamid Razak, Mr Melvin Yong and others had also raised questions about the veterinary workforce.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I shared earlier that the Council will continue to implement continuing professional education requirements for vets to renew their practising certificate, to equip them with up-to-date knowledge, skills and experience.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: AVS also provides scholarships and study grants for students to pursue vet programmes and contribute to our pipeline of vet professionals.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Beyond this, AVS and the Council will partner stakeholders, such as MOE and the IHLs, to strengthen veterinary-related formal education programmes or training provided locally, including those that may allow mid-career entrants into the sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our review also includes manpower projections and resource requirements to study the need and feasibility of a local vet degree programme.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying also asked about occupational support.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While the Protection from Harassment Act protects all individuals, including vets, from harassment, AVS will also work with the Council to explore other initiatives to improve workplace practices and professional development opportunities to better support our vets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also intend to eventually extend registration to other vet professionals, such as vet nurses.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While they are not currently licensed by AVS today, we will continue to engage our vet sector before developing the regulatory framework for them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In line with Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Yip Hon Weng's suggestions, we will also monitor the impact of the enhanced set of regulations to vets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will update on the registration timeline for other vet professionals when we are ready.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Meanwhile, the Bill will clarify the scope of vet activities and circumstances where non-vets may perform them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For instance, vet nurses will be allowed to perform certain vet activities under supervision by a duly qualified vet and in accordance with any prescribed conditions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This requirement to be supervised is already in place today.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Council will also publish guidelines before the commencement of the relevant provisions next year, setting out the broad principles of the appropriate supervision.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To Mr Muhaimin Malik's questions, we share your concerns about community animals and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I have many of them in my constituency as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To our community caregivers, please continue to care for your animals as you already do, but please also exercise judgement when you need to refer them or to bring them to a vet.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The third theme of questions that Members have raised relate to penalties and disciplinary proceeding provisions as prescribed by the Bill.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, Mr David Hoe asked how penalties under the Bill were derived.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: AVS will continue to regulate animal health and welfare, and offences involving animal welfare and cruelty will continue to be dealt with under the ABA.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As Members know, and I have said that in public and in this House, we are reviewing the penalties for animal welfare offences and the licensing regime for pet sector activities, including pet grooming businesses under the ABA.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, we have established a robust disciplinary framework, including a range of disciplinary orders that may be imposed on errant vets to strengthen deterrence against professional misconduct.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I shared earlier how the Bill establishes clear escalation thresholds in handling complaints and how the various committees can make orders to deal with professional misconduct.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is unless the Council, on application by the Complaints Assessment Committee or Disciplinary Committee, allows otherwise.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To Mr Muhaimin Malik's questions about resourcing for enforcement, NParks currently undertakes the enforcement of the existing vet licensing framework and will continue to support the Veterinary Council as we transition to the new framework.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also wish to assure Assoc Prof Jamus Lim that NParks has strict protocols around evidence gathering and investigations, and works with other agencies, where practical and necessary, to gather information to support its investigations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Third, Ms Diana Pang asked why there is no requirement for a legal professional to be in the Interim Orders Committee.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Where necessary, legal professionals can be appointed to the Interim Orders Committee, as clauses 4 and 39 respectively provide for laypersons, such as legal professionals, to be represented in the Council and the complaints panel.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Clause 65 also provides for the Council to appoint an advocate and solicitor to prosecute the disciplinary case, or to advise the Interim Orders Committee on any legal matter relating to the inquiry or review.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are also safeguards for vets before the Interim Orders Committee.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Before the Council appoints any independent expert, it must give the registered vet concerned an opportunity for him or her to make representations on the proposed appointment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The vet may also appeal to the General Division of the High Court against the Interim Orders Committee's decision.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And all interim orders are also subject to periodic review, to ensure no order remains in force longer than is necessary.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked if the enhanced disciplinary proceedings could result in the sector becoming overly litigious and if vets may feel pressured to adopt defensive practices to protect themselves.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The limitation period for complaints also ensures that cases brought before the Council are supported by timely and reliable evidence.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, there will be clear escalation thresholds in the handling of complaints.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Registrar will objectively assess and triage each case, and can recommend dismissal of frivolous complaints to the Council, so vets are not unduly burdened by cases without merit.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
